# From Prompt to Physics: Evaluating a Doppler Effect Simulation Generated by ChatGPT

**Ghonia Millata Mallia Shofa et al.** · 2026 · *Physics Education* 61(1), 015029
**DOI:** 10.1088/1361-6552/ae272c (IOP Publishing)
**Domain:** LLM-generated science simulations — evaluation · **Verified:** ✅ IOPscience DOI, volume,
issue and article number confirmed
**Priority:** ⭐ reusable evaluation instrument

## What it does
Develops a Doppler effect simulation through iterative prompt engineering — attending to interface,
user experience, wave visualisation, and accuracy of the physics representation — then evaluates it
via **self-evaluation and expert evaluation using a Likert scale plus qualitative analysis**.
Results: maximum scores on both conceptual accuracy and visualisation; limitations found in
interface flexibility. Concludes ChatGPT has considerable potential for developing physics
simulations, with ongoing evaluation necessary for educational appropriateness.

## Why it matters to Synapse
The most directly reusable artifact in the whole set: **a published, peer-reviewed rubric for
judging whether a generated science simulation is any good**, separating conceptual accuracy from
visualisation quality from interface usability.

That decomposition maps cleanly onto what a Synapse evaluation needs to measure, and borrowing an
instrument from a published physics-education journal is far more defensible than inventing a rubric
two days before a deadline. It also means an expert-rater design (rather than a learner-outcome
study) is an accepted methodology in this literature — which matters, because a learner study is not
happening by 20 August.

Being in *Physics Education* also gives the reference list genuine cross-disciplinary range: an IOP
science-education journal alongside ACL/ACM/arXiv reads as a properly situated paper rather than a
pure CS submission wearing an education label.

## The gap it leaves
n=1 simulation, one topic, evaluated after human-guided iterative prompting. It measures whether a
*carefully shepherded* generation can be good, not whether generation is *reliably* good — and
certainly not whether it is safe unsupervised. The authors' own conclusion that "ongoing evaluation
is necessary" is an unresolved dependency on human effort.

## How to cite it
Evaluation (rubric design and justification) and Related Work (prior evaluation of generated science
simulations). One of the highest value-per-word citations available.
